description: Team SARamba | Challenge: Dancing with the SARs. We'll use NASA-ISRO NISAR radar to reveal the water hidden under the Amazon rainforest, which regular satellites can't see through the clouds. I'm a developer focused on AI, automation and web apps (React, TypeScript, Python). Idea, 48h plan and datasets already mapped. Looking for: a geospatial/Python data person (rasterio, QGIS), a front-end dev (React, maps) and a designer/storyteller for the pitch. Let's make NASA's jaw drop!
summary: SARamba is a web app that uses the L-band radar of the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission to show the water hidden under the Amazon forest canopy. In the Anavilhanas archipelago (Rio Negro, Brazil), the forest floods every year, but optical satellites see only clouds and a uniform green canopy. NISAR passes through both. We processed all eleven NISAR passes of one orbit, from high water (June 2026) to low water (October 2026), classified open water and flooded forest from HH backscatter, and compared the result with the official river level at Manaus. The area classified as flooded forest fell from 379 km² to 30 km² while the river dropped from 28.5 m to 16.5 m. The app lets anyone drag a slider between the cloudy optical image and the radar image of the same day, step through the dates, see a map of how long each place stayed flooded, and click any point to read its radar signal over time, with the limits of the method stated on screen.
details:
What it does. SARamba opens on a slider: on the left, a Sentinel-2 optical image of the Anavilhanas archipelago taken on 18 June 2026, with 53% of the window under cloud or cloud shadow; on the right, the NISAR L-band HH image acquired on the same day. Dragging the slider replaces clouds with a sharp picture of the river, its islands and very bright fringes along islands and creeks. A timeline switches between eleven radar dates, one every 12 days. Other layers show:

  • a three-class map (open water, flooded forest, not flooded on that date);
  • a flood duration map: on how many of the eleven dates each pixel was classified as flooded forest;
  • a change map between the first and the last date.

A chart plots flooded forest area, with an uncertainty band, against the Rio Negro level at Manaus. Clicking any point on the map shows the HH signal of that place across the eleven dates. A four-card story mode walks a first-time visitor through the idea. The interface is available in English and Portuguese.

How it works. L-band radar penetrates clouds and forest canopy. Over open water the signal is reflected away and the image is dark. Under flooded forest the signal bounces between the water surface and the tree trunks (double bounce) and returns strongly in HH polarization, so flooded forest is brighter than forest on dry ground.

The pipeline (Python) does the following for each date:

  1. reads a 50 × 50 km window from the NISAR L2 GCOV product (frequency A, HHHH, terrain-corrected gamma0, 20 m grid);
  2. averages 2 × 2 pixels in power (40 m) and applies a 5 × 5 Lee speckle filter;
  3. converts to decibels;
  4. classifies each pixel from HH with two thresholds calibrated once on the histogram of all dates together: open water at or below −11.37 dB (two-class Otsu) and flooded forest at or above −3.65 dB (mode of the non-flooded forest peak plus two standard deviations measured on the uncontaminated side of the peak);
  5. recomputes the flooded area with the threshold moved by ± 0.5 dB, to show how much the result depends on it;
  6. computes the area of each class, a transition map between the first and the last date, and the number of dates on which each pixel was flooded;
  7. exports small PNG and JSON files.

Only scenes from the same orbit (path 68, frame 90, descending) are compared, so the viewing geometry is identical on every date. Five of the eleven passes recorded HH+HV and six recorded HH only; the classification uses HH, so all eleven are used. The web app (React, TypeScript, MapLibre GL, Recharts) only reads the pre-computed files, about 24 MB in total, and keeps working without an internet connection.

Between June and the end of October, 360.1 km² changed from “flooded forest” to “not flooded”. In total, 566.6 km² were classified as flooded forest on at least one date and 209.8 km² on six or more. Across the eleven dates, flooded area and river level have a Pearson correlation of 0.97. Both fall through a single dry season, so a high value is expected; it is consistent with the flood receding under the canopy and is not proof.

Benefits. Flooded forests feed fish, store carbon and set the calendar of river communities, and they are under cloud for most of the high-water season. A radar that returns every 12 days regardless of weather can follow the flood pulse where optical monitoring cannot. SARamba makes that visible to a non-specialist in a few seconds, turns a stack of passes into a single flood-duration map, and keeps the method simple enough to be checked and repeated.

Limitations. The NISAR products used are provisional (calibrated, still under validation). Eleven dates of one season indicate a trend, not statistical proof. Thresholds come from the image histogram only; there is no field validation. The absolute area is sensitive to the threshold, as the band in the table shows, although the direction of the trend is not. Other bright targets can be labelled as flooded forest. The series is not strictly monotonic (17 August is higher than 24 July) and we did not investigate why. The river level is measured at Manaus, downstream of the archipelago, and is raw telemetry. These limits are stated in the app and in the README.

Tools. Python (asf_search, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, pyproj, rasterio, Pillow), TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Recharts, GitHub Pages. Open source under the MIT license.
